Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the Apex Insurance Group Fourth Quarter and Full-Year 2023 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Johnson: Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Apex Insurance Group's Q4 and full-year 2023 earnings call. Joining me on the call today are Johnathan Hale, Chief Executive Officer; Michael Reynolds, Chief Financial Officer; Lisa Chen, Chief Underwriting Officer; David Patel, Chief Investment Officer; and Robert Kline, Chief Operating Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we are making today may be considered forward-looking. These statements are subject to certain risks and uncertainties that could cause our actual results to differ materially from those projected. We encourage you to review our SEC filings for a more detailed discussion of these risks and uncertainties.

I will now turn the call over to Johnathan Hale.

Johnathan Hale: Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. I'm pleased to report on Apex Insurance Group's performance for the fourth quarter and full year 2023. We delivered strong results, driven by robust dividend payments reflecting our progressive policy, a fortified capital position with substantial statutory surplus growth, strategic asset allocation yielding resilient returns, elevated policy retention rates across major lines, favorable changes in actuarial assumptions boosting reserves, and improving loss ratio trends amid disciplined claims management. We are particularly excited about the initial success of our AI-driven parametric insurance product and its positive impact on catastrophe risk mitigation and customer retention.

Michael, our CFO, will now provide a more detailed review of our financial performance.

Michael Reynolds: Thank you, Johnathan. Good morning, everyone. As Johnathan mentioned, we had a solid quarter and full year. Our net income was $1.2 billion for the quarter, or $7.45 per share on an adjusted operating basis. Key drivers of our financial performance included strong underwriting discipline, elevated investment yields, favorable prior-year reserve development, and prudent capital management. Our combined ratio was 92.4% for the full year—our best since 2019—despite $450 million in pre-tax catastrophe losses from events like Hurricane Idalia and California wildfires.

Before we move deeper into the results, I'd like to spend a few minutes on our dividend policy and the Board's recent declaration, as it's a key pillar of our capital allocation framework and a testament to the strength of our franchise. As you know, Apex has a proud history of delivering consistent and growing dividends to shareholders, underpinned by our disciplined underwriting, robust investment portfolio, and fortress-like balance sheet. Today, I'm pleased to announce that our Board of Directors has declared a quarterly dividend of $0.82 per share on our common stock, payable on March 15th to shareholders of record as of February 28th. This marks a 2.5% increase from the prior quarter's $0.80 and represents the 12th consecutive quarterly increase, bringing our annualized dividend to $3.28 per share—up 6.5% year-over-year.

Let me put this in context with some key metrics. At our current stock price of around $102, this translates to a forward dividend yield of approximately 3.2%, which remains competitive within the large-cap P&C peer set—think Chubb at 1.4%, Travelers at 2.1%, and Progressive hovering below 0.5% due to their growth focus. Our trailing 12-month payout ratio stands at a prudent 44% of adjusted operating EPS of $7.45, well within our target range of 40-50%. This leaves ample room for reinvestment while prioritizing shareholder returns. Looking at trends, our dividend per share has compounded at a 7.2% CAGR over the past five years, outpacing inflation and even the S&P 500 Insurance Index's average yield growth. This growth has been fueled by several tailwinds, including our consolidated combined ratio of 92.4% for FY23, driven by rate adequacy across our core P&C lines where we achieved mid-single-digit earned premium growth.

On the investment side, our $145 billion portfolio delivered a 4.8% total return in 2023, bolstered by our fixed income ladder yielding 4.2% and selective exposure to investment-grade munis and corporate bonds amid the Fed's rate hike cycle. This generated $5.2 billion in net investment income, up 12% YoY, providing stable cash flows to support our payout. Regionally, our U.S. operations—the heart of our P&C book—saw dividend-supporting profitability with a 91.8% combined ratio, aided by personal auto rate hikes averaging 9.2% and commercial multi-peril renewals up 7.5%. In Europe, our Lloyd's syndicate delivered a standout 85% combined ratio, benefiting from benign weather and our focus on specialty risks like cyber and D&O, where we grew premiums 15% while maintaining attritional loss ratios below 60%. Asia-Pacific, our growth engine via life and health reins, contributed meaningfully too, with embedded value growth of 11% from our bancassurance partnerships in Japan and Southeast Asia.

Strategically, this dividend hike reflects our confidence in sustaining ROE above 15%—we hit 16.2% in Q4—and our RBC ratio of 620%, giving us significant excess capital of about $4.2 billion post-dividend. We're balancing this with $1.5 billion in share repurchases YTD under our $3 billion authorization, at an average price of $98, yielding 2.1% to total shareholder yield. Looking ahead, we expect to maintain our progressive dividend policy, targeting 5-8% annual growth, supported by ongoing technical initiatives. These include our AI-driven catastrophe modeling platform, which reduced our nat cat tail by 18% through better peak peril pricing—integrated with RMS and AIR Worldwide models—and our shift to parametric reinsurance structures, locking in $2.8 billion of cover at favorable terms with partners like Swiss Re and Munich Re. In life & health, our longevity swap program has de-risked $3 billion in annuity reserves, freeing up capital for distribution.

We're also monitoring macro headwinds like persistent inflation in repair costs—up 5.2% in auto—and social inflation in liability lines, but our 102% reserve redundancy and agile pricing discipline position us well.

Turning now to our capital position and statutory surplus levels, which remain a cornerstone of our financial strength and flexibility. In the insurance industry, maintaining a robust capital base is critical not only for regulatory compliance but also for supporting organic growth, pursuing strategic M&A opportunities like our recent bolt-on acquisition of Midwest Specialty Lines, and returning capital to shareholders amid volatile market conditions. Let me start with the headline numbers under statutory accounting principles, or SAP, as reported to the NAIC. At year-end 2023, our consolidated risk-based capital, or RBC, ratio stood at a very strong 458%—well above our internal target of 400% and the regulatory "company action level" of 200%. This represents a 22 percentage point improvement from 436% at the end of 2022, despite absorbing approximately $650 million in net catastrophe losses from events like Hurricane Idalia and the Maui wildfires, which were partially offset by favorable prior-year reserve development of $420 million.

Our statutory surplus grew to $16.2 billion, up 9.2% year-over-year from $14.8 billion. This marks the 17th consecutive quarter of surplus growth, driven by a combination of underwriting profitability, higher investment income from our fixed-income portfolio yielding 4.8% in 2023—benefiting from the Fed's rate hiking cycle—and disciplined expense management. Excluding AOCI impacts from rising rates, adjusted surplus growth was even stronger at 11.5%. Book value per diluted share, on a non-GAAP operating basis, increased 12% to $48.50, underscoring the quality of our earnings.

Diving into segment details, our Property & Casualty, or P&C, operations—which represent 65% of surplus—posted an RBC ratio of 512%, up from 485% last year. This resilience held firm even as we navigated a 102.3% calendar-year combined ratio in Personal Lines Auto, pressured by social inflation and repair costs up 15% YoY. Commercial Lines, however, delivered a pristine 94.2% combined ratio, fueled by rate adequacy gains of 8.7% and strong retention above 92%. In Life & Annuity, our RBC stands at 385%, supported by sales of fixed indexed annuities totaling $2.8 billion in VA alternatives, which have lower capital charges under the upcoming LDTI framework.

Regionally, our U.S. statutory entities remain rock-solid, with the lead P&C surplus pool at $11.4 billion and an RBC of 475%, easily passing all state-specific L'Hartwig collateral tests. Internationally, our Bermuda operations—key for our excess & surplus lines platform—grew surplus 14% to $2.1 billion, leveraging sidecar reinsurance to derisk cat exposures. In Europe and Asia-Pacific, where we're expanding cyber and parametric products akin to those from AXA XL or Swiss Re, surplus rose 7% to $2.7 billion, though we saw modest pressure from UK motor claims inflation.

On technical initiatives, we've proactively managed capital through our annual reinsurance renewals. At the January 1st renewal, we placed $4.2 billion in cat reinsurance coverage, including quota shares on our $15 billion gross cat limit, at flat-to-1% improved terms thanks to our superior loss ratio track record. We've also accelerated our transition to model-agnostic approaches under ORSA, incorporating climate risk scenarios from RMS v18 models, which has unlocked $300 million in RBC relief. Additionally, our capital optimization program includes $500 million in pension de-risking via longevity swaps with PIMCO, reducing tail risks.

Strategically, this capital fortress positions us exceptionally well. We've deployed $1.2 billion YTD toward growth, including dividend growth to $1.05 per share (up 8%) and $800 million in share repurchases at an average of $42 per share, accretive to book value. Looking ahead, with projected 2024 EPS growth of 10-12% and organic combined ratio improvement to 97%, we expect RBC to expand toward 470-490% and surplus growth of 8-10%. We're also evaluating opportunistic M&A in the $5-10 billion range, targeting P&C run-offs similar to our Enstar partnership, while maintaining payout ratios below 50% of operating earnings. In summary, our capital position not only exceeds peer medians—think Travelers at ~420% or Chubb at 450%—but provides the dry powder for value creation in a hardening market.

As we dive deeper into our investment portfolio performance, I'd like to provide a comprehensive overview of our asset allocation strategy, which remains the cornerstone of our asset-liability management—or ALM—framework. Our portfolio, totaling $285 billion as of quarter-end, is designed to deliver stable, risk-adjusted returns while ensuring we meet our policyholder obligations under various stress scenarios, including those modeled in our economic capital framework and Own Risk and Solvency Assessment, or ORSA.

Let me start with the high-level snapshot. Our strategic asset allocation target remains 72% fixed income, 15% equities, and 13% alternatives. At quarter-end, we were positioned at 73% fixed income, 14% equities, and 13% alternatives—a slight overweight to fixed income driven by tactical deployment of cash flows from maturing bonds amid the ongoing yield curve normalization. This compares to 75% fixed income, 12% equities, and 13% alternatives a year ago, reflecting our deliberate pivot toward equities as valuations corrected post-2022 drawdown.

Year-to-date, the portfolio generated a total return of 4.2%, outperforming our benchmark—the Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Bond Index blended with the MSCI World Equity Index at 60/40—by 120 basis points. This was fueled by carry in fixed income and selective equity gains, partially offset by mark-to-market pressures in longer-duration assets. Our book yield stands at 4.1%, up 25 basis points quarter-over-quarter, supported by reinvestments at higher rates.

Fixed income continues to anchor our portfolio, with an average duration of 5.8 years—precisely matched to our intermediate-tail liability profile, where 65% of reserves are due within 10 years. We maintain a high-quality bias: 85% investment-grade, including 40% U.S. Treasuries and agency MBS, 25% IG corporates, and 20% public and private securitized products like CLOs and ABS. Regionally, our U.S. allocation dominates at 55% of fixed income ($114 billion), benefiting from the Fed's terminal rate around 4.75-5% and resilient corporate spreads at 105 basis points over Treasuries. We've layered in $12 billion in short-duration TIPS to hedge inflation risks, yielding 2.1% real. In Europe, 25% ($52 billion), we're navigating ECB rate cuts—now at 3.5%—by tilting toward peripheral sovereigns like Italian BTPs (spread 140 bps) and covered bonds, which offer 4.2% yields with low volatility. Asia-Pacific, at 15% ($31 billion), emphasizes JGBs and AUD corporates amid BOJ normalization, where we've initiated a $2 billion yen carry trade hedged via FX forwards.

Technically, we've advanced our portfolio optimization with AI-driven credit selection models, integrated with BlackRock's Aladdin platform, which screened 15,000 issuers to identify 200bps excess spread opportunities in BBB-rated sectors like utilities and renewables. We also deployed $1.5 billion in interest rate swaps to extend duration selectively, locking in 4.5% synthetic yields. Q3 new money yields averaged 4.8%, versus 3.9% a year ago, but we're cautious on further rate volatility—our VAR at 99% confidence is $2.8 billion, well within our 150bps spread risk appetite.

Equities provide the necessary return kicker to combat longevity risk in our life and annuity blocks, targeting 7-9% long-term returns. We're at 60% U.S., 25% developed international, and 15% emerging markets. U.S. exposure is concentrated in the S&P 500 via low-cost ETFs like Vanguard's VOO, with overweight to financials (25% of equity sleeve) mirroring peers like Berkshire Hathaway's model—think JPMorgan and Chubb for their superior ROEs above 15%. Performance-wise, equities returned 8.5% YTD, led by tech rebound (Microsoft, Nvidia holdings up 25%), but we've trimmed cyclicals post-summer rally. Internationally, Europe lagged at 4% due to energy sector weakness, prompting a 2% rotation into UK gilts-equity hybrids. In EM, our $6 billion stake—focused on India and Brazil via iShares MSCI EM ex-China ETF—delivered 12% amid commodity tailwinds, though we're monitoring China's property overhang.

Strategically, we've embedded ESG overlays, with 40% of equities in sustainable funds like BlackRock's iShares ESG Aware MSCI USA, aligning with NAIC climate risk guidelines. Options overlays generated $150 million in premium income, reducing beta to 0.85. Compared to Allianz's more aggressive 20% equity tilt, our conservative stance preserved RBC ratios above 450%.

Alternatives are our secret sauce for uncorrelated returns, targeting 6-8% IRRs to support P&C cat reserve build-up. Breakdown: 40% private equity ($15 billion), 30% real assets ($11 billion), 20% hedge funds ($7 billion), and 10% infrastructure ($4 billion). Private equity, via funds from KKR and Apollo, vintage 2021-2023, is at 1.4x MOIC with DPI of 0.25x—strong distributions from exits in healthcare. Real estate, 60% core U.S. multifamily and logistics (Prologis partnerships), yielded 7.2% levered, hedging inflation via 3% annual escalators. Hedge funds, macro and event-driven via Citadel and Millennium, returned 5.1% with low correlation (0.2 to IG bonds).

Regionally, North America is 70%, Europe 20% (focusing on data centers amid AI boom), and Asia 10% (renewable projects in India). We've ramped illiquidity premium capture to 150bps via a $3 billion direct lending program to mid-market insurers. Initiatives include tokenization pilots with Goldman Sachs for fractional real estate ownership, enhancing liquidity, and GP stakes for 20% fee rebates. Illiquids now contribute 25% of portfolio income, up from 18% YoY.

Looking ahead, we're guiding for modest fixed income overweight into 2025 as rates peak, with equity re-risking if 10-year yields stabilize below 4%. ALM stress tests—incorporating 200bps parallel shift and equity 30% drop—confirm surplus coverage above 120%. We're exploring cat bond issuance via our Bermuda reinsurer for alternatives diversification, targeting $500 million, and advancing duration extension via green bonds to meet EU SFDR reporting. This disciplined allocation not only drove 15% ROIG—return on invested assets—but positions us resiliently amid geopolitical tensions and election uncertainty. Our portfolio beta to GDP growth is 0.6, far below the industry average of 0.9 per AM Best data.

Shifting to operational metrics, one of our key leading indicators of profitability and growth is policy retention rates by major product line. Retention remains the bedrock of our book of business, directly impacting our loss ratio stability, expense leverage, and long-term combined ratio. For the quarter, our company-wide retention rate stood at 89.2%, up 140 basis points year-over-year and marking our 11th consecutive quarter of sequential improvement. This outperforms the industry composite of 87.5% as reported by AM Best for personal lines and SNL Financial for commercial, reflecting our disciplined pricing, enhanced customer servicing, and targeted retention initiatives.

In personal lines auto insurance, our TTM retention improved to 88.7%, a 210 bps gain from a year ago, driven by our next-gen telematics program, 'DriveSafe Insights,' now active with over 4.2 million policyholders—that's 62% penetration in our book. Similar to Progressive's Snapshot but with AI-powered behavioral coaching via our app, this has reduced claim frequency by 12% for participating drivers and boosted loyalty among millennials and Gen Z, who represent 45% of our new auto writings. Regionally, U.S. retention hit 90.2%, benefiting from rate adequacy amid 8-10% inflation in repair costs, while our European book—primarily UK and Germany—held steady at 85.4%, pressured by softening market pricing from competitors like Aviva and AXA. In Australia, post-flood recovery, we're at 87.9%, with bundling discounts for auto-home combos lifting cross-sell penetration to 32%. Strategically, we're layering in predictive analytics from our partnership with Verisk Analytics to flag at-risk policies 45 days pre-renewal, intervening with personalized offers. This has yielded a 3.5% uplift in retained premium, offsetting the 2-3% voluntary lapse from rate increases averaging 9.2% this year.

Homeowners retention remains our strongest suit at 91.3% TTM, up 90 bps YoY, well above the industry average of 88% per NAIC data. This resilience stems from our parametric trigger enhancements for wildfire and hurricane perils, tested successfully during California's 2023 fire season and Florida's Hurricane Idalia. We've seen a 15% reduction in non-renewals from catastrophe-exposed policyholders by auto-adjusting deductibles and offering micro-insurance riders. U.S. Southeast retention is at 89.8%, challenged by reinsurance cost escalation post-Ian, but we've clawed back to 92.5% in the Midwest through our 'Smart Home Shield' IoT integration with partners like Google Nest, which qualifies customers for up to 18% discounts and has driven 28% attachment rates. In Canada, our book—focused on multi-peril dwellers—achieved 93.2%, aided by regulatory tailwinds from OSFI's emphasis on climate risk disclosure. Looking ahead, we're targeting 92.5% TTM by year-end via expanded usage-based pricing.

Commercial lines property & casualty retention is a standout at 93.4% TTM, gaining 160 bps YoY and surpassing peers like Chubb (92.1%) and Travelers (91.8%) per their latest disclosures. Middle-market accounts under $5M in premium—our sweet spot—retained at 95.1%, fueled by our 'Enterprise Risk Optimizer' platform, which uses machine learning to benchmark client exposures against RMS catastrophe models, reducing mid-term cancellations by 22%. Regionally, U.S. retention is 94.7%, with strength in the Northeast industrial corridor, while Asia-Pacific dipped to 90.2% due to supply chain disruptions in manufacturing classes. Our UK commercial book, hit by the Cost of Living crisis, stabilized at 92.8% through flexible installment billing and ESG-linked premium credits. Key initiative here: We've rolled out API integrations with ERP systems like SAP for 1,200 large accounts, automating certificate management and slashing service lapses. This, combined with pricing discipline—mid-single-digit increases on 78% of renewals—positions us for a sub-95% loss ratio in H2.

Workers' comp retention rose to 92.1% TTM, up 120 bps, reflecting proactive return-to-work programs and telemedicine partnerships with Teladoc, which cut indemnity costs by 11% and improved broker satisfaction scores to 4.7/5.0. In the U.S., experience mod refinements for high-hazard classes like construction yielded 93.5% retention, while Australia lagged at 89.4% amid labor shortages. Strategically, we're emphasizing pay-for-performance wellness incentives to push toward 93.5% by FYE. Rounding out the portfolio, our life and annuity block—22% of in-force—posted 94.6% TTM retention, bolstered by lapse-protected universal life products and indexed annuity riders amid rising rates. This compares favorably to Prudential's 93.2% peer average.

Overall, these retention gains have added $450M to our annualized in-force premium, supporting our raised 2024 combined ratio guidance of 92-94% and EPS outlook of $7.85-$8.15. Risks include catastrophe loading from an active Atlantic season—we've purchased $2.5B in excess-of-loss reinsurance at attractive terms—and competitive pricing wars in auto. Our tech roadmap includes full rollout of GenAI chatbots for renewal triage by Q4, targeting another 100-150 bps lift in 2025. We're also exploring embedded insurance via partnerships with fintechs like Stripe to acquire sticky policies at lower cost.

As we unpack the details behind our strong reserve dynamics and earnings trajectory, one key driver this quarter was changes in our actuarial assumptions and their impact on our financials. We recognized a net favorable impact of $285 million pre-tax from assumption updates across our Life & Annuity and Group Benefits segments—that's about 15 basis points of positive contribution to our operating ROE and roughly 8% of our adjusted operating income.

At Apex, we maintain a disciplined annual assumption study process, grounded in emerging experience data from our $450 billion in-force book, benchmarked against Society of Actuaries tables like the 2023 CSO mortality update and the International Actuarial Association's longevity projections. We also incorporate stochastic modeling via our proprietary Dynamic Risk Engine—a machine learning-enhanced platform that's reduced assumption uncertainty by 25% since its 2022 rollout, using over 10 petabytes of telematics, claims, and socio-economic data. This isn't static; it's dynamic, with quarterly reviews triggered by thresholds like 5% experience variances or macroeconomic shifts.

Starting with mortality and morbidity assumptions, which drove the lion's share of this quarter's favorability. In our U.S. individual life portfolio—anchored by our flagship TermLife Pro and Universal Life products—we updated base mortality rates downward by 2.5% on average, reflecting post-COVID normalization. 2021-2022 saw excess mortality spike 18% per CDC data, but our 2023 experience showed a 12% favorable deviation versus priced-in assumptions. This unlocked a $180 million reserve release in Q2, primarily on our $120 billion term and whole life blocks. For annuities, improved smoker/non-smoker gradients—informed by our partnership with Verisk Analytics—added another $65 million, as lapse-adjusted persistency hit 92% versus our prior 88% assumption. On the flip side, morbidity in Group Health crept unfavorable by 1.8%, driven by higher utilization in mental health claims amid ongoing workforce stress—up 14% YoY per our claims dashboard. This resulted in a $35 million charge, but it's more than offset by the mortality tailwinds and aligns with industry trends seen at peers like UnitedHealth and Cigna.

Next, lapse and policyholder behavior assumptions saw a modest unfavorable shift: surrender rates on fixed annuities increased to 7.5% from 6.8%, reflecting competitive pressure from rising Treasury yields—the 10-year now at 4.3% versus our 2023 average pricing at 3.2%. This hit our $80 billion deferred annuity book for a $45 million reserve build. However, offset by stronger than expected anti-selectivity in variable annuities, where crediting rate floors held firm amid equity volatility (S&P 500 up 12% YTD but with VIX spikes). Net, policyholder behavior contributed +$20 million favorable.

Discount rates and economic assumptions were a standout. With the Fed's terminal rate now embedded at 4.5% in our base case—up from 3.0% last year—we boosted our long-term discount rate by 45 basis points to 4.2% for life reserves. This alone released $95 million, echoing moves by Prudential and MetLife in their recent 10-Qs. We stress-tested this under 1,000 LDI scenarios using our Monte Carlo engine, ensuring tail-risk coverage for a 200bps parallel shift.

Regionally, this plays out differently. In North America (75% of our book), the updates were broadly favorable, juiced by U.S. longevity deceleration—our 2023 experience showed life expectancy gains slowing to 0.8 years per decade versus the SOA's prior 1.2-year trend, thanks to obesity and opioid headwinds. Europe (15% of book) saw a $40 million net charge: UK prudence under Solvency II forced a 10bps higher risk margin on our £15 billion with-profits fund, while French morbidity worsened 3% on post-strike healthcare delays. EIOPA's 2024 longevity calibration, which we adopted early, added conservatism here. Asia-Pacific (10%) was the bright spot—+$35 million favorable from Japan's ultra-low lapse rates (4.2% vs. 5.5% assumed) on our JGAAP-compliant whole life sales, up 22% YoY amid yen weakness boosting repatriation demand. Emerging markets like India contributed via updated ICMA morbidity tables, reflecting telemedicine efficiencies that cut claims severity 9%.

Strategically, these changes underscore our "Assumption Agility" initiative—a $150 million, three-year tech investment blending AI-driven nowcasting (predicting experience 12 months ahead with 85% accuracy) and blockchain-secured data sharing with reinsurers like Swiss Re and Munich Re. This positions us ahead of regulatory headwinds.

Finally, on underwriting performance, let's focus on loss ratio trends and the key drivers behind them—specifically claims frequency and severity—which remain central to our disciplined approach to profitability in this volatile P&C landscape. For the quarter, our consolidated loss ratio came in at 91.2%, a 330 basis point improvement from 94.5% in Q3 2022, and down 110 basis points sequentially from Q2's 92.3%. This marks our best quarterly loss ratio since Q1 2021, pre-COVID disruptions, and puts us on track for a full-year 2023 combined ratio of approximately 96.5%, within our guided range of 96-97%.

Frequency saw a modest 1.8% decline quarter-over-quarter on a per-exposure basis, driven by favorable trends in auto and workers' comp, partially offset by weather-related upticks in property. In Personal Auto, which represents 42% of earned premiums, frequency fell 3.2% YoY, thanks to our expanded telematics adoption—now at 28% penetration in our book, up from 18% a year ago. This mirrors industry leaders like Progressive's Snapshot program, allowing us to refine risk selection and price high-frequency drivers more aggressively.

Severity, however, remains the bigger headwind, up 4.7% YoY on an indexed basis, aligning with broader social inflation pressures. Repair costs for vehicles have surged 12% due to persistent supply chain issues with OEM parts—think semiconductor shortages lingering from the auto chip crisis—and labor rates hitting $55 per hour in key markets like California and Texas. In Property, severity spiked 6.1% amid a benign cat year so far, but we're lapping last year's Hurricane Ian losses, which drove $1.2 billion in industry-wide claims. Our ex-cat property loss ratio held steady at 62.4%, reflecting proactive reinsurance renewals at the January 1 layers, where we secured 40% quota share coverage on Florida wind exposure at favorable terms.

Regionally, the U.S. P&C book delivered a standout 89.8% loss ratio, down from 93.2% YoY, fueled by auto frequency normalization post-pandemic driving rebound—fewer miles driven per telematics data dropped 4% from peak 2021 levels—and our GLMs incorporating machine learning for better loss cost projections. In contrast, our Commercial Lines saw a 95.6% ratio, pressured by 5.2% workers' comp severity inflation from rising medical costs and litigation trends; OSHA fines and attorney involvement in California alone added 150 basis points to reserves. Internationally, Europe contributed positively with a 87.1% ratio in our UK motor and liability portfolios, benefiting from softer frequency amid economic slowdowns—claims per policy down 2.5%—though German flood residuals from 2021 events kept severity elevated at +3.8%.

On the technical front, we're leaning into several initiatives to counter these drivers. First, our AI-powered claims triage system, rolled out in Q2, has reduced cycle times by 22% and flagged 15% more subrogation opportunities, directly shaving 40 basis points off the loss adjustment expense ratio. Second, we've embedded climate risk modeling from partners like RMS and AIR Worldwide into our cat aggregation tools, enabling a 10% reduction in peak U.S. property exposures in high-risk zones like Florida and Louisiana. Pricing discipline is key here: we took mid-single-digit increases across 85% of our renewing auto book, with rate adequacy now at 105% per our internal metrics, outpacing peers like Travelers and Chubb.

Strategically, this positions us well for 2024. We're optimizing our portfolio by non-renewing $250 million in underperforming small commercial excess & surplus lines, redirecting capital to high-return D&O and cyber products where loss ratios are sub-85%. Reinsurance cost moderation—our ceded ratio stable at 28% despite Benfield tower adjustments—combined with reserve releases of $45 million this quarter from favorable prior accident year development, gives us tailwinds. Looking ahead, we expect Q4 loss ratio in the low 90s, assuming normalized weather, but remain vigilant on severity amid 3-4% projected medical CPI and auto repair escalation. Overall, these trends underscore our focus on actionable underwriting intelligence over reactive adjustments.

We continue to maintain a strong capital position, with RBC at 620%. Lisa, over to you for more on underwriting.

Lisa Chen: Thank you, Michael. I'd like to provide an update on our underwriting performance. We've seen continued strong performance in our commercial lines business. We are actively managing our exposure to catastrophe risks and have implemented several initiatives to improve our risk selection, including advanced AI catastrophe modeling and parametric reinsurance structures that have materially reduced our tail risks.

David Patel: Thank you. From an investment perspective, we have continued to focus on diversifying our portfolio and managing risk in the current market environment. We are seeing positive returns from our investments in high-quality fixed income and selective alternatives, as Michael detailed, which have supported our overall yield enhancement.

Operator, we are now ready to open the line for questions.

Operator: Thank you. [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from Emily Carter with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Emily Carter: Good morning. Can you provide more color on the drivers behind the dividend increase and how sustainable is the 5-8% growth target?

Johnathan Hale: Good morning, Emily. Absolutely. As Michael outlined, the hike to $0.82 reflects our underwriting improvements, investment income growth, and excess capital position. With ROE at 16.2% and payout at 44%, we have plenty of flexibility. The 5-8% target is sustainable given our technical margin expansion from AI tools and reinsurance optimization, positioning us to grow dividends progressively while funding growth and buybacks.

Operator: Our next question comes from David Lee with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

David Lee: Good morning. Could you discuss the impact of persistent inflation on your business, particularly repair costs and social inflation?

Michael Reynolds: Good morning, David. Inflation remains a headwind, with auto repairs up 5.2-12% and social inflation in liability lines. We've countered this with 9.2% auto rate hikes, machine learning in GLMs for precise pricing, and claims triage reducing LAE. Our loss ratios improved to 91.2% despite this, and we expect continued discipline to keep combined under 97% in 2024.

Operator: Our next question comes from Rachel Kim with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Rachel Kim: What is the expected impact of upcoming regulatory changes like LDTI and Solvency II updates on your underwriting strategy?

Lisa Chen: Good morning, Rachel. LDTI will lower capital charges on our fixed indexed annuities, freeing up surplus for growth, while Solvency II enhancements in Europe prompt more conservative risk margins, which we've already baked in with early adoption. Our strategy emphasizes model-agnostic ORSA approaches and climate-integrated pricing, ensuring resilience. We've stress-tested reserves accordingly, with net favorable assumption changes supporting our position.

Operator: Our next question comes from Tom Vargas with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Tom Vargas: Thanks. On retention, how are you thinking about the competitive landscape in personal auto, and any updates on telematics penetration?

Lisa Chen: Hi Tom. Retention at 88.7% TTM reflects our telematics edge at 62% penetration, driving 12% frequency reductions. Competition is softening rates in some markets, but our AI coaching and Verisk analytics flag at-risk policies early, yielding 3.5% premium uplift. We expect further gains from GenAI chatbots.

Operator: Our final question today from Susan Patel with BlackRock.

Susan Patel: Good morning. Regarding asset allocation, any shifts planned for alternatives amid higher rates?
